rv.q: Magic/Bird piqued my interest in seeing a more illuminating documentary about their lives and careers, but it fails to weave those elements into anything more than a mildly engaging drama.

Their brief, volatile encounter turns out to be the most dramatic moment in “Magic/Bird,” an efficiently informative but uninspired trek through the lives of two towering (forgive the pun) figures in sports history.
As vividly as the actors inhabit their parts, Eric Simonson's story is a bit too thin for Broadway.
Tasteful to a fault, the play is unlikely to offend anyone, particularly the National Basketball Association or Johnson, both involved in producing.
The uneventful play ultimately resembles an audiovisual presentation of a Wikipedia article.
This warm and funny passage is characteristic of the entire play, which smoothly melds abundant humor, human details and basketball lore to chronicle an unlikely real-life bromance.
The plodding pace, greatest-hits superficiality, and hagiographic tone of 'Magic/Bird' feels jarringly dated.

cn.t: Critics find this NBA drama about Magic Johnson and Larry Bird sanitized and dramatically flat, with a lifeless script that fails to justify the stage as a medium, though some praise the game footage and lead performances.

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.

acc.note: Small restroom-only elevator (may not accommodate all wheelchairs). 3 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra.
